competitors.name: SimpleClosure (AssetHub)
competitors.what_they_do: Funded shutdown-services company whose AssetHub marketplace sells or licenses code, workspace archives, data and domains of dissolving companies, and licenses data for still-operating companies. AI labs are 'among the most active buyers'. The asset report already says buyers want 'manufacturing, energy, banking and insurance, professional services and logistics' data. It offers valuation, curation and de-identification, excludes sensitive employee/comp/health data, and is building WorkSpace (beta). Its H1 2026 report frames customers as VC-backed startups, but its 2023 TechCrunch profile says it serves 'startups, corporations, and LLCs'. Its marketing already targets the exact verticals in this idea, so it is the most likely incumbent to widen its funnel.
competitors.scale_or_funding: $1.5M pre-seed in 2023 (Vera Equity, Cambrian Ventures; https://techcrunch.com/2023/09/06/simpleclosure-raises-1-5m-to-companies-shut-down-faster-and-cheaper/). Later funding not verified. Reported deals are tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars, and The Verge covered the data-sale launch (https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/913806/this-startup-sells-dead-company-data-for-ai-training).

competitors.name: Sellmybusinessdata.com
competitors.what_they_do: Finds valuable data inside a company, de-identifies a private copy and brings the owner offers from AI buyers, with no sale unless the owner says yes. Target industries listed: healthcare, manufacturing, logistics, accounting, legal, finance, insurance, construction, distribution, professional services. Data sources include Slack, Teams, Gmail, SAP, Salesforce, QuickBooks, Drive, SharePoint and operating records such as orders, invoices and logistics data. Fee is '$0 upfront, we participate only when you accept an offer and the deal closes'. This is nearly the same offer to nearly the same customers, but it is not focused on closures and has no visible broker/CPA channel.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Operator not identified on the site and no funding info found. Commission percentage not disclosed.

competitors.name: Troveo
competitors.what_they_do: Data-licensing marketplace that now runs a business-data vertical. It scopes archives, strips personal details, packages and licenses them to AI buyers. Its business data covers ITSM, CRM, customer support, financial ops and inventory systems. It explicitly pitches closing companies and takes no fees or deductions from seller payouts, positioning against closure platforms that take a cut. It also says it has 40+ active buyers, and its site claims 350+ enterprise data-provider companies (unverified).
competitors.scale_or_funding: About $4.5M seed (Reddit and Zynga founders) per its homepage. Claims $20M+ paid to 7,000+ rights holders, mostly video/audio/gaming. Cites deal ranges of about $5K per repository and $10K-$100K per startup archive.

competitors.name: FileYield
competitors.what_they_do: Private brokered marketplace for proprietary AI training data. Sectors include manufacturing, financial services, legal and customer service. It names OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, Anthropic, Amazon, Scale AI and Databricks among buyers (self-reported, unverified). It charges 8% to sellers and 6% to buyers, far below the proposed 25-35%.

competitors.name: Opendatabay
competitors.what_they_do: General licensed data marketplace for AI training and fine-tuning datasets (text, code, robotics, medical, synthetic). Sellers list datasets themselves. No sign it handles closing-company operational archives, so it is a channel and price anchor rather than a closure broker.

competitors.name: Court-supervised liquidation auctions (Spirit Airlines model)
competitors.what_they_do: Large bankruptcies already sell data estates through court-run auctions. Google paid $10M, pending judicial approval, for 100M+ emails, 500M Teams items, 30M+ recorded calls, 763K+ flights of ops data, 1.2M fuel slips and 787K parts purchases. Mercor was the underbidder. This proves the top of the market but is not a repeatable SMB service. Traditional liquidators such as Hilco and Heritage Global could add data-asset lines, but I found no evidence that they have.

white_space:
The idea's core claim is that Main Street firms have 'nobody to appraise or sell their data'. That is now false in general. Sellmybusinessdata.com, Troveo and FileYield all pitch AI-buyer data sales to manufacturing, logistics and insurance firms. SimpleClosure's asset report names the same verticals. What I found nobody doing:

(1) Closure-event channel. No one is embedded in the workflows of business brokers, CPAs, liquidators, ABC assignees and Chapter 7/Subchapter V trustees who handle non-VC small-business closures. Those advisors have a fiduciary or client-service reason to surface an overlooked estate asset. The competitors are direct-to-seller or startup-founder-led.

(2) Time-critical capture. The data is destroyed when the QuickBooks/ERP/email/TMS subscriptions lapse and owners retire. A closure-triggered preservation and rights-clearing workflow is different from a generic 'sell your data' page.

(3) Vertical-specific packaging. Examples are freight-broker quote/dispatch/TMS logs or machine-shop RFQ, quote and work-order sets matched to named buyers building vertical agents. The competitors are horizontal.

(4) Insolvency-grade rights review for non-consumer-PII operational data. The competitors' rights and de-identification work is generic and consumer-PII-adjacent.

The proposed pricing is a weakness. A 25-35% fee plus a $500-1,500 scan competes against $0 upfront (Sellmybusinessdata), 0% seller fee (Troveo) and 8% (FileYield). Reported startup archive deals run $10K-$100K, so 30% of a small machine shop's corpus may not cover rights-review and packaging costs.
evidence_of_demand:
Buyer-side demand is real. Seller-side and non-tech demand at meaningful prices is not yet proven.

Buyer-side:
- Google paid $10M for Spirit Airlines' data, with Mercor as underbidder (https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/18/google-buys-crashed-airline-spirits-data-at-auction-because-ai/5288962). The HN thread had 616 points (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49343559).
- SimpleClosure says AI labs are among the most active AssetHub buyers, sees 'demand for data in industries like manufacturing, energy, banking and insurance, professional services and logistics', and reports deals of tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/what-your-assets-are-worth/ and https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/state-of-shutdowns-h1-2026/).
- Troveo says it has 40+ active buyers, a business-data vertical, and quotes $10K-$100K per startup archive (https://troveo.ai/resources/sell-startup-assets-to-ai-labs).
- Press coverage: The Verge (https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/913806/this-startup-sells-dead-company-data-for-ai-training) and Forbes (https://www.forbes.com/sites/annatong/2026/04/16/ais-new-training-data-your-old-work-slacks-and-emails/). I saw only headlines and snippets, because both pages blocked fetching.

Weak spots:
- SimpleClosure notes its current dataset is dominated by developer tools and infrastructure, and it says buyers 'want' scarce industries. I found no closed deal in manufacturing, freight or insurance.
- HN commenters doubt de-identification (AOL 2006 precedent, writing-style re-identification) and suggest Scale, Surge and Mercor build synthetic 'simulated companies' rather than buy real records.
- I found no RFPs, regulations forcing spend, or forum complaints from small-business owners or brokers asking for this service.

Limitation of this research: the session's WebSearch budget (200) was exhausted before my first query. Findings rest on direct fetches of the idea's cited sources and competitor sites, plus a few search-result pages fetched through WebFetch. No Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt sweep was possible, so the competitor list may be incomplete.
kill_reason: n/a. Not killed, but this is a low-confidence pass. The generic 'data broker for non-tech firms' concept is crowded, and only the narrow closure-channel, vertical-packaged wedge survives. The conclusion is not yet stress-tested against a full Crunchbase/YC/Product Hunt sweep, which was not possible here.
sharper_angle:
Do not pitch 'data broker for Main Street'. Pitch closure-event infrastructure sold to the professionals who already run non-VC wind-downs, in one vertical, with a buyer committed first.

1. Distribution moat. White-label a 'data asset addendum' for business brokers, CPAs, liquidators and insolvency trustees or ABC assignees. It is a 30-minute intake plus a rights checklist added to the closing checklist, with a referral split for the advisor. Trustees have a duty to maximise the estate, and this asset is currently ignored.

2. Speed and preservation. Freeze and export ERP, TMS, quoting and email data before subscriptions lapse. Do the rights and de-identification work once per source system (for example one TMS or one CAD/quoting stack), so every later closure on that stack is near-zero marginal cost.

3. Buyer-first, one vertical. Start with freight brokerage or machine-shop quoting. Sign 2-3 vertical-AI buyers to standing purchase or acquisition agreements before recruiting sellers. Consider charging buyers a data-acquisition retainer instead of taking 25-35% from thin seller estates.

4. Price against the market. Drop the $500-1,500 scan (competitors are $0 upfront) and move to a success-only fee in the 8-20% band, or a flat trustee fee paid from proceeds. At 25-35% the idea is undercut by FileYield (8%), Troveo (0% to sellers) and Sellmybusinessdata ($0 upfront).

5. Kill test before building. Get three signed listing agreements from brokers or trustees and one buyer LOI at a stated price for a specific corpus. If no buyer pays for small-shop operational data at a price that clears the cost of rights review, drop the idea. The unproven point is the value of non-tech SMB data, not the existence of AI buyers.
